title: [Autour de La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois, pages 1 à 67] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp. 50–51 of the 'Longue Marche' manuscript notes, c. 1981). k is a field (later of finite type over Q). K is the fraction field of a henselian discrete valuation ring with inertia group T. U is a hyperbolic curve of type (g,ν) over K, and π = π_1(U_{η̄}) is the profinite 'π à lacets' (surface group). Two exact sequences are in play: (30) 1→π→π_1(U)→E_K→1, and (31), its restriction to the inertia/decomposition part. A K-rational point of U gives a splitting of (31) and hence a homomorphism T→π.

The previous page lists candidate conditions on U:
- a) U has good reduction.
- b) The (outer) action of inertia T on π is trivial, i.e. (31) splits suitably.
- c) T acts trivially on π_ab = H_1(U_{η̄}).
- d) T acts trivially on H_1(U_{η̄}, T_ℓ) for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. For ℓ = p, Grothendieck suggests a criterion via p-divisible groups.
- e) For k of finite type over Q, given two sections of (30), the extension of E_k by π they define is 'admissible': it comes from geometry, being definable by an algebraic curve over k or a finite extension of k.
- f) For a section of (30) and one of (31), the resulting action of E_k on π is 'not too wild', to be defined.

This page states:
1. Obviously a ⇒ b ⇒ c ⇒ d.
2. d ⇒ a 'should be more or less known', or provable from well-known results such as Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich / Serre–Tate together with semistable reduction (SGA 7).
3. These conditions imply e). But he has no idea how to show e) ⇒ good reduction; that would need a deeper, presumably arithmetic, understanding.
4. He extracts a 'general principle', to be formulated in proper generality. One can construct (more or less natural) outer actions of the Galois groups E_k (k of finite type over Q) on surface groups π that are presumably NOT geometric, by using curves of type (g,ν) that have bad reduction. The idea is to combine a geometric Galois action with inertia data coming from a badly-reducing curve, producing an action that cannot come from any curve.

The next page breaks off this approach ('je ne m'arrête pas par cette voie'). It reformulates the goal as an exercise: produce effective outer actions, built from geometric ones, which are not themselves geometric, of the two types 1°, 2° considered at the start of the section.

The problem served is to characterize which outer Galois actions on π_1 of hyperbolic curves are 'geometric' (come from curves). This is an anabelian analogue of asking which Galois representations are geometric.

The diagonal marginal note is largely illegible. It mentions something like 'x+y = …' (perhaps a Fermat-type or tripod example), a reduction condition, and 'dégénérées'. It appears to suggest testing the idea on degenerate or explicit examples.
errors: The claim that d) ⇒ a) 'should be more or less known' is false as stated for curves of genus ≥ 2. Trivial inertia action on H_1(U, T_ℓ) (or on π_ab) only gives good reduction of the Jacobian. A curve whose stable reduction is of compact type (e.g. two elliptic curves meeting in one point) has bad reduction but satisfies c) and d). The correct criterion uses the outer action on the full (pro-ℓ) fundamental group: Oda (1990/1995) for proper curves, Tamagawa (1997) for affine curves. Thus c) and d) are strictly weaker than a), b) in general.
For open curves (ν > 0), condition d) on H_1 is even weaker because of the boundary/cusp contributions. Again only the nonabelian condition b) characterizes good reduction (Tamagawa).
Hence the chain a ⇔ b ⇔ c ⇔ d asserted implicitly here is wrong. Only a ⇔ b (with the right formulation of b, outer pro-ℓ inertia action trivial) holds.

ideas.what: Criterion for good reduction of a curve via triviality of the inertia action on its fundamental group
ideas.usually_credited_to: T. Oda (1990, 1995); A. Tamagawa (1997) for affine curves

ideas.what: Abelian version: trivial inertia on H_1 / Tate module
p-adic analogue of the good reduction criterion via p-divisible groups
ideas.modern_name: Crystalline criterion for good reduction (Fontaine, Coleman–Iovita, Breuil)

ideas.what: Condition e): which extensions of Galois groups by π (from pairs of sections) are 'admissible', i.e. come from algebraic curves; open question whether this forces good reduction
ideas.modern_name: Geometricity of outer Galois actions; related to the section conjecture and to anabelian 'Fontaine–Mazur'-type questions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (section conjecture, 1983 letter to Faltings); geometricity questions treated by Mochizuki, Tamagawa and others

ideas.what: Principle for constructing non-geometric outer actions of Galois groups of fields of finite type over Q on surface groups, using curves with bad reduction
ideas.modern_name: Construction of non-geometric outer Galois representations on π_1 of hyperbolic curves

missed.claim: Grothendieck proposes a general principle: build natural outer actions of E_k (k of finite type over Q) on surface groups that are not geometric, by gluing in inertia behaviour from badly-reducing curves. He also asks whether 'admissibility' (e) implies good reduction. This is a nonabelian analogue of the Fontaine–Mazur question of which Galois representations are 'geometric', with local conditions at bad primes as the obstruction. As far as I know, no systematic theory characterizing geometric outer actions on π_1 of hyperbolic curves by local conditions has been developed.
missed.quote: J'ai donc là un principe général ... pour construire des actions ± naturelles de groupes E_k ... sur des π à lacets, qui (sans doute) ne soient [pas] géométriques, par la considération de courbes de type (g,ν) "se réduisant mal".
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: An 'anabelian Fontaine–Mazur' framework is a live but underdeveloped topic. This page shows Grothendieck already in 1981 framing geometricity of nonabelian Galois actions in terms of local reduction behaviour and explicitly seeking non-geometric examples.

missed.claim: This is an early (pre-Oda) formulation of the good-reduction criterion via inertia acting on π_1. It wrongly suggests that the abelian condition on H_1 would suffice. That makes it historically interesting as a precursor to the Oda–Tamagawa criterion, where the nonabelian nature is exactly the point.
missed.quote: évidemment a) ⇒ b) ⇒ c) ⇒ d), et d ⇒ a devrait être plus ou moins connu
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical credit: it shows Grothendieck considered the π_1-inertia criterion for good reduction around 1981, a decade before Oda.

deep.surprise_reason: There is an unpublished early formulation of the Oda-type good reduction criterion, alongside a sketched programme for constructing non-geometric Galois actions on surface groups via bad reduction (an anabelian Fontaine–Mazur flavour). However, the abelian part is erroneous, and the construction is only announced, not carried out.
transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'ou du moins [?] facile [?] de prouver' is probably 'ou du moins [facile] à prouver à l'aide de choses bien connues'.
'il faudrait une compréhension (fond. elle [?] arithmétique [?])' is probably '(fondamentalement arithmétique)'.
'qui (sans doute) ne soient [?] [-du-] {+la+} géométriques' should read 'qui (sans doute) ne soient pas géométriques'.
Insertion over 'extérieures': the struck word is likely 'extérieures' replaced with '± naturelles'; the actions are still outer actions.
'(k corps de type fini sur Q)' is correct; the printed 'E_k' in the image matches 'E_h' / 'E_k' on the previous page.
The last line likely reads 'Mais je n'insiste pas', continuing as 'pas par cette voie' on the next page.
